Two of the world's most powerful regulatory bodies just admitted the same thing in the same week: they do not fully understand what AI is doing to their economies. And they are acting anyway.

On July 16, the European Commission detailed Digital Markets Act requirements that would force Google to provide greater interoperability with AI competitors. Days earlier, the Federal Reserve established an AI task force under Marc Andreessen, acknowledging that AI's economic effects — strong productivity gains, soft white-collar hiring, and an investment boom running on borrowed electricity — are genuinely difficult to parse.

For executives, this is not background regulatory noise. It is the beginning of a structural shift in how AI platforms will be required to operate. The DMA interoperability mandate means that walled-garden AI ecosystems are on a regulatory clock. If your product strategy depends on a single platform's AI capabilities, the ground underneath it is about to move.

The companies that build platform-agnostic AI integrations now will have optionality when interoperability mandates take effect. The ones that wait will scramble to re-architect under deadline pressure.

Regulatory foresight is not compliance overhead. It is strategic positioning.
